title: Storing Functions in Modules
objective: Reuse code across files by organizing functions into importable modules.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.chapterTitle: Functions (Storing Functions in Modules); Classes (The Python Standard Library)
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: A module is just a Python file whose functions and variables another file can borrow with import. Once a function proves useful in more than one place, moving it into its own module keeps your programs from repeating themselves.

import module_name loads the whole module; you reach its contents with module_name.function_name(). from module_name import function_name pulls a single name in directly, so you can call function_name() without the prefix.

You can rename what you import with as — either the whole module, written import module_name as alias, or a single name pulled from it, written from module_name import function_name as alias. Renaming is handy for long names or for avoiding a clash with something you already defined. from module_name import * pulls in everything at once instead — avoid it, because it hides where each name came from and can silently overwrite names you already have.
explanation.rule: Import only the names you need, and use as when a shorter name makes your code clearer.

examples.title: How a Module Import Would Look
examples.code:
# --- geometry_helpers.py ---
def square_area(side):
    return side ** 2


# --- main.py ---
# import geometry_helpers
# from geometry_helpers import square_area as area_of_square
#
# print(geometry_helpers.square_area(4))
# print(area_of_square(4))

print(square_area(4))
examples.note: geometry_helpers.py would hold just the function. The commented lines in main.py show two real ways to reach it: import the whole module and use the dotted name, or import the function directly under a shorter alias. Code Forge runs everything as one file, so square_area is already defined above and the final line calls it directly.

checks.question: Why is `from module import *` usually avoided?
options: It runs slower than a normal import.
It pulls in every name from the module at once, hiding where each one came from and risking accidental overwrites.
It only works with the math module.
Python does not actually allow it.

feedback.correct: Correct — star imports make it hard to trace where a name came from and can quietly replace names you already defined.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think about what happens when every name in a module suddenly appears in your file at once.
